Work Description: 
 
Con Edison is currently working on the Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) project from 2016-
2022 as per the current business case, which involves the implementing the IT platform, building 
communication network, and installing over 5 million electric and gas Smart Meters. This initiative 
comes at a time when New York State is seeking to rethink and improve its energy future. The Con 
Edison AMI smart meter initiative is integral to this very effort, and it is the most influential and 
transformational project in the company’s history. 
 
The Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) environment supports critical corporate applications, 
hosting smart meter data and asset information for customer billing, outage management, and other 
purposes. This includes the Meter Data Management system (MDMs), Meter Asset Management 
system (MAMs), Profield (our Smart Meter installation and support software) and the server and 
hardware consisting of over 120 servers and storage located at various Con Edison and vendor hosted 
data centers. Included in the AMI environment and this supported infrastructure are the development, 
test, parallel, and user production environments, supporting the AMI platform and serving the various 
business units whose primary work assignments is to ensure accurate bills are delivered to our 
customers.  
 
The AMI computer environment also functions as a platform for and will be redesigned to support 
CORE (Oracle’s CC&B), customer information system replacement project, Gas Central gas work 
management system project, and the replacement of the existing CECONY and O&R mainframe 
systems. Vital billing determinants gathered in the AMI computer environment will be used to ensure 
the new CORE system continues to provide customers accurate billing information. 
 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 2 of 43


--- Page 547 ---
2 
 
The hardware supporting the AMI platform is designed with redundancy and resiliency in mind. This 
in order that our commitment of 15-minute interval meter reads across all 5.3 million meters are 
obtained on time without impacting billing processes which in turn produce customer bills. 
 
After the completion of the major AMI Business case in 2022, the plan is to improve existing business 
processes and eliminate manual processing. As part of this capital request (2024-2026) it is to support 
software enhancements to the Meter Data Management (MDMs), Meter Asset Management system 
(MAMs) and Profield systems. The focus for this request will be centered around the need for 
continuously improvement and stabilization in the area of billing, asset management and meter, 
network devices and sensor events processing. The enhancements above will also ensure we continue 
to support of ongoing corporate initiatives around meter data, sensor data and outage data dependent 
on AMI business strategy. This includes the Outage Management System, which is dependent on AMI 
for smart meter status during storm events processing, in turn limiting restoration time and reducing 
truck rollouts.   
 
Secondly, in order to ensure we are current with software version for vendor support as well as latest 
cyber security requirements.  Hence the MDM system need to be upgraded to the latest version during 
this capital request (2024 – 2026).  
 
Finally, there is a need to replace all existing AMI hardware supporting Con Edison hosted AMI 
systems (this includes 300 file servers and the supporting disk storage required to maintain customer 
meter information) in year 2024 – 2026 as the current life span of the hardware and support expires in 
2024.  
 
Our production systems located at our 30 Worth Street production data center provide the computer 
hardware to support the consumption of 5.3 million meter reads , collecting the data in 15 minute 
intervals. As part of our commitment to our customers this information is also required for data 
presentment to all Con Edison customers. In addition, and as part of our commitment to improve in 
the area of accurate customer billing, our goal is to reduce and potentially eliminate the need to 
estimate customer bills.  
 
In order to accomplish this the replacement hardware will need to be designed and implemented with 
high availability infrastructure for the Meter Data Management  (MDMs) system,  this both at our 
production data center at 30 Worth Street and also the disaster recovery site in Secaucus. Once 
implemented we anticipate a significant improvement on the overall billing process and a reduction of 
manual work which allows for human error. 
 
 
Justification Summary: 
As part of the deployment of 5 million electric and gas Smart Meters and enhancements to the AMI 
network, the elimination of manual work will improve safety for our customers and enhance the user 
operational experience. The planned system enhancements include introducing new software which 
will allow for real time alerts to be sent to first responders in the event of a menthane sensor failure or 
an actual gas leak.   
 
Additionally, the AMI project will be seeking to implement new operational improvements throughout 
2023-2026. For example, the AMI/Information Technology (IT) department will seek to further 
optimize interfaces between MAMS, MDMS, CC&B, and Gas Central. Furthermore, it is advantageous 
for Con Edison to consolidate interfaces feeding meter exchanges to CORE and AMI is preparing to 
retire or expand the Profiled Encore application to meet that projected need. Lastly, the MDMS will be 
perform another upgrade (9.0) in late 2025 for the MDMS to stay in compliance with security patches.

efforts to keep CORE and the AMI infrastructure in sync which supports accurate and timely billing

Project/Program Title: AMI Business Analytics  
Project/Program Manager: Berna Falay Ok    
Project/Program Number (Level 1): 23322950 
Status:  ☒ Initiation  ☐ Planning  ☐ Execution  ☐ On-going  ☐  ☐ Other:  
Estimated Start Date: March 2022 
Estimated Date In Service: December 2025 
A. Total Funding Request ($000)  
Capital: $7,179 
O&M: $300 
 
B.  
☐ 5-Year Gross Cost Savings ($000) 
☐ 5-Year Gross Cost Avoidance ($000)

D. Investment Payback Period:   
(Years/months) (If applicable) 
Work Description: 
 
The goal of this project is to design and deploy a suite of data analytics use cases to assess customer 
load profiles and patterns while leveraging the Company’s Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) 
data, as well as other internal and external data sources. This integrated application (AMI Business 
Analytics) will allow Con Edison to gain predictive insight into specific customer trends, reconciliation 
of weather adjusted peaks of the gas and electric systems, and uptake of load modifiers. It will also 
help the system planning process, which is designed to identify current and future operating 
requirements, risks, and potential solutions to provide safe, reliable, and resilient systems.   
 
This effort will leverage the Company’s Enterprise Data Analytics Platform (EDAP), which will 
provide information about these systems that dictate the use cases of the model.  The program will 
identify additional analytics to be performed on the data already existing in EDAP, as well as the 
opportunity to integrate new data sources to unlock additional insights and deliver new analytics use 
cases. The project will focus on data integration for customers employing emerging technologies like 
electric vehicles (EVs), heat pumps, distributed energy resources (DG/CHP), and other systems 
incentivized by policies like New York States’ Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act 
(CLCPA) and New York City’s Local Law 97 (LL97). 
 
Initial use case scenarios listed below are mostly concentrated around emerging technologies and new 
business/growth, but as the project matures, Energy Management/Commodity  
Forecasting will continue to build upon these use cases to address emerging policy and innovation and 
to reflect continuous improvement. The effort will establish a framework for identifying new use cases. 
It will also assess value delivered relative to complexity and reprioritize the portfolio of use cases as 
appropriate.  The effort will begin by examining the following use cases: 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 7 of 43


--- Page 552 ---
2 
 
 
Use Case 1: Electric Vehicle and Chargers Load Profiles:  
As EVs gain traction in the marketplace, they will require the installation of charging infrastructure. 
The chargers, which have varying charging speeds based on wattage requirements, are a large 
investment in and of themselves. Depending on where the demand to charge vehicles manifests, they 
may have a large effect on network and system peak and volume. Increases in electric demand could 
require Con Edison to coordinate heavily with EV charger installers prior to adding a charger to the 
grid and might even lead to eventual upgrades to the distribution system. Planning for the mass 
adoption of EVs is therefore necessary. 
 
The project will examine details on how EVs impact the load peak and load curves in Con Edison’s 
networks. The Company will analyze the AMI data to create a typical load curve for the following 
breakout categories:  
• 
Light, medium, and heavy-duty vehicles, 
• 
Publicly accessible charging stations (e.g., those in parking garages) and privately held stations 
(e.g., those in private residences, 
• 
Level 1 chargers (L1), Level 2 chargers (L2), and direct current fast chargers (DCFC). 
Analyzing these load curves alongside adoption estimates will help to forecast the effect EV chargers 
will have on both networks and the distribution system. 
 
Use Case 2: Heat Pumps: 
Like EVs, heat pumps are being promoted as alternatives to gas fired boilers and furnaces. Con Edison 
anticipates that in coming years, new business customers will likely install electric space heating 
systems and that existing buildings will retrofit their heating systems to comply with emissions limits. 
Heat pumps, which can be used in space- or water-heating systems, will play a key role in the 
electrification of heating because of their potential to make electric heating more efficient. However, as 
with EVs, the impact heat pumps have on peak and volume for both gas and electricity are difficult to 
determine without knowing how heat pumps operate within the Con Edison territory. Because the 
heat pump coefficient of performance is dependent on ambient temperature and because existing 
studies on heat pump performance have tended to take place in climates that are much warmer than 
that in the Northeast, there is a dearth of relevant, useful data regarding heat pump performance. The 
Company must therefore attempt to discover their load behavior using customer AMI information so 
that it can improve its forecasting accuracy. Energy Management plans to use AMI data of customers 
who have installed heat pumps to gain a better understanding of how they function on the Company’s 
distribution system. It will examine load performance in the following different categories:  
• 
Air source heat pumps for new and existing buildings 
• 
Ground source heat pumps for new and existing buildings 
• 
Hot water system heat pumps for new construction and retrofits. 
 
Use Case 3: Battery Storage: 
Con Edison is partnering with companies to ensure that battery storage is being installed in the 
territory. In some cases, these batteries have not yet seen significant use, but they are the forerunners in 
what will be a movement toward storage interconnection. The owner of the battery technology and the 
purpose it is meant to serve will determine its actual behavior. Energy Management/Commodity 
Forecasting plans to use AMI Business Analytics application to develop a nuanced understanding of 
the load behavior of batteries with respect to their operational objectives. 
 
Use Case 4: New Business Ramp Up 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 8 of 43


--- Page 553 ---
3 
 
AMI could also provide insight on new business ramp-up electric usage. New construction can 
sometimes take several years from beginning to completion, incurring a slowly increasing electric 
demand. Eventually the electric demand from a building will achieve a demand in line with design 
expectations communicated to Con Edison. Prior to that point, however, it is important to know the 
percentage of its projected load that new construction is incurring. AMI hourly data from prior 
projects’ ramp up can provide estimates as to when new business reaches its peak demand after 
completion. Using AMI history from ongoing projects, Energy Management/Commodity Forecasting 
intends to link usage data to different types of construction documented in customer accounts. This 
will allow for a territory-specific ramp-up electric load curve. Energy Management/Commodity 
Forecasting plans to develop typical load curves based on the location and building type of new 
construction to assist in the development of electric peak forecasts at the network level. This is critical 
for our load relief planning.  
 
Use Case 5: New Business Load Density 
AMI data could provide Energy Management/Commodity Forecasting with the opportunity to 
analyze the electric load of new buildings that have been connected to the distribution system and use 
their ramped-up demand to get an estimate of average load density for buildings. Energy 
Management/Commodity Forecasting intends to calculate a load density in kVA per square foot for 
different customer types and different building types. This will give it a critical load value that it will 
employ in long-term forecasting. 
 
Use Case 6: Gas Load Distribution of Interruptible Customers 
Energy Management/Commodity Forecasting will use AMI data from interruptible gas customers to 
understand what the customers’ typical hourly loads are and how much gas those customers use each 
day. This will assist Gas Forecasting in developing a more accurate forecast for interruptible gas usage. 
Analyzing AMI data in conjunction with account information for interruptible customers will also 
allow Energy Management/Commodity Forecasting to study the results of peak events during which 
interruptible customers are required to use an alternate source of fuel. Studying these events would 
give Energy Management/Commodity Forecasting a better understanding of when and how 
interruptible customers contribute to peak gas demand. It could allow them to predict how many of 
the customers will reliably comply with their alternate-fuel agreement. This will reduce the uncertainty 
of the weather adjusted peak and add value to its annual reconciliation to the forecast. 
 
In addition to these high-priority case uses, Energy Management/Commodity Forecasting will be able 
to use EDAP to assess the impact that Energy Efficiency and Demand Response programs have on 
demand. The group will also integrate AMI data from distributed generation customers, such as, for 
example, distributed solar output. 
 
Justification Summary: 
 
Recent policies such as the CLCPA and LL97 have significantly increased the importance of the utility 
planning process and therefore have put upward pressure on the accuracy of the short, medium, and 
long-term forecasting of the electric, gas, and steam systems. In support of the CLCPA goals, the 
Company must be prepared to leverage the capabilities of clean energy technologies including EVs, 
heat pumps, Battery Storage, and Solar Panels (PV), to enable a dynamic and reliable grid. This project 
will help enhance the variety of reporting, analytics and forecasting that the Energy Management 
Organization provides to both internal and external customers. Energy Management, which is 
responsible for wholesale energy transactions, billing and reporting to different markets and 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 9 of 43


--- Page 554 ---
4 
 
regulatory bodies, also provides short, medium, and long-term electric, gas and steam forecasts. These 
forecasts include peak, volume, and revenue forecasting. 
 
The Company’s existing data sources and platforms can be leveraged to create business value to 
address these challenges. These include but are not limited to: EDAP, Customer Project Management 
System (CPMS), Demand Management Tracking System (DMTS), Customer Information System (CIS), 
Power Clerk, EnergyIP/MDMS, MV90, and TCIS.  
 
This project will help Energy Management perform the following functions: 
 
• 
Integrate AMI data into the existing forecasting process flow to allow for more accurate 
representation of load growth, better visibilities into impacts and participation in energy efficiency 
programs and customer energy usage behaviors at more granular levels. 
• 
Consolidate data sources used by Energy Management into a single platform. 
• 
Utilize state-of-the-art software to improve Energy Management in managing approximately $3.5 
billion in wholesale energy transactions. 
• 
Plan for future needs that arise from the CLCPA, LL97, and Reforming the Energy Vision (REV) 
using a fully integrated solution for AMI data analytics. 
• 
Use advanced software, automation tools and advanced analytics to move away from time-
consuming manual processes. 
 
Improving the Company’s knowledge of the future helps it to optimize capital and O&M expenses by 
making existing processes more efficient and reproducible. It also contributes towards the Company’s 
Clean Energy Commitment; these use cases give the Company the opportunity to plan for a green future 
and provide a positive impact to the customer. Other potential impacts could include managing or 
preventing an increase in customer rates and improving system performance with targeted programs 
implemented in response to data analytics.  
 
A lack of understanding of customer behavior and load modifier adoption could result in inaccurate 
forecasts, increase the risk exposure of system reliability and supply cost, and lead to misalignment with 
environmental and energy policies. 
 
Relationship to Broader Company Plans and Initiatives (e.g. Long-Range Plans, CLCPA Initiatives, 
Risk Mitigation) 
 
The Company’s five- and ten-year plans include preparing for a green energy future as outlined in 
LL97 and in the CLCPA. This project addresses CLCPA investment activity by implementing an AMI 
Business Analytics tool that addresses use cases aligned with CLCPA goals. For example, the CLCPA 
includes goals to install 3,000 MW of battery storage by 2030. Con Edison is seeking to approve 
interconnection requests for at least 300 MW of storage in its service territory by 2025. AMI Analytics 
that examine the performance of batteries currently installed on the system provide Con Edison with 
an understanding of where batteries can be deployed based on their performance and where they 
might be most useful.  
 
Similarly, use cases addressing the additional load incurred by heat pumps will provide a fundamental 
understanding of technology that will help to decarbonize New York State. AMI Analytics will help to 
develop forecasts, which predict what Company revenue will be. Knowledge of revenue helps to build 
a budget that looks five years into the future and includes plans to implement these technologies. 
Understanding them now is therefore critical to Company function and climate mitigation. 
 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 10 of 43


--- Page 555 ---
5 
 
Improving energy usage analytics also helps the Company to mitigate risk. Insufficient information 
regarding emerging technologies leads to inaccurate commodity forecasts. Because forecasts are used 
to plan energy purchases and operational projects, they can negatively impact the Company’s strategic 
plans. Inefficient scheduling or operational work could result in increased customer bills, decrease in 
Company reliability, and negatively impact stakeholder relations. The inverse is also true; better 
forecasting can help to manage customer costs, improve visibility of problem areas that the Company 
must address, and improve the stakeholder experience. AMI analytics can act as a powerful tool for 
forecasting improvement that the Company has identified as a key risk mitigation initiative.  
2. Supplemental Information 
 
Alternatives 
 
Alternative 1 
 
One alternative would be to continue existing processes without incorporating AMI data into the 
workflows. This alternative would fail to leverage critical customer data from one of the Company’s 
largest investments. It also has the potential to lead to inaccurate forecasting. Lastly, running manual 
one-off queries is time-consuming, complicated and is not an ideal, efficient or effective option.  
 
Alternative 2 
Another alternative is to reduce the scope of the AMI Business Analytics undertaking so that it does 
not address as many use cases as laid out in the Work Description. The inability to leverage AMI’s  
valuable data could result in the Company not adequately addressing high priority forecast modifiers, 
whose effects are not yet holistically quantified. Energy Management / Commodity Forecasting has 
deemed the use cases listed above as vital to producing an accurate long-term forecast that complies 
with CLCPA demands.  
 
 
Risk of No Action 
 
Risk 1 
Various parts of the Company are already beginning to use AMI data to support their operations and 
decision-making process. If Energy Management does not take advantage of this opportunity, the 
department will lag in utilizing data to drive decisions and not reap the benefits of one of the biggest 
investments the Company has taken. 
 
 
Risk 2 
As the Company’s gains more data from AMI and as more customers elect to install new electric 
technologies, the traditional methods of forecasting load become increasingly insufficient. The more 
time spent without a way to incorporate AMI data into predictions, the less accurate those predictions 
are likely to be. This runs the risk of inaccurate revenue predictions, inaccurate O&M and capital 
forecasts, decrease in system performance, poor customer experience, and potentially increased cost to 
the customer. 
 
 
Non-Financial Benefits 
 
This tool allows for the development of advanced analytics, which will provide new insights for the 
Company and its customers. The insights provided by advanced analytics will have indirect benefits to 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 11 of 43


--- Page 556 ---
6 
 
improving the customer experience, providing valuable information to the Company to make 
informed strategic decisions as it relates to its capital strategy, where to deploy operations and 
maintenance resources, and where to prioritize upgrades to improve system performance. This project 
will also help the state meet its clean energy goals to ensure the state has a green future.  
 
 
Summary of Financial Benefits and Costs (attach backup) 
1. Cost-benefit analysis (if required) 
This project will indirectly result in financial benefits, as mentioned above. Accurate forecasts lead to 
improved dispatch and procurement of gas and electric supply and meeting load with the appropriate 
amounts. An under-forecast could lead to purchasing electric and gas in the real time market at a 
premium and an over-forecast could lead to purchasing too much gas or electric.  
  
 
2. Major financial benefits 
 
In addition to the financial benefits previously mentioned, this new application will lead to improved 
daily, peak, and volume forecasts, which can help optimize costs and planning. 
 
 
3. Total cost 
 
The total capital cost of this project is $7.2 million, which includes procurement / development of 
software, algorithmic coding, and labor associated with gathering requirements, designing, 
implementing, testing, and deploying the suite of data analytics use cases.  
 
 
4. Basis for estimate 
 
The capital costs are based on an estimation model for analytics work derived from prior analytics 
efforts.  The model takes into account the number of new data sources to be integrated into EDAP; the 
transformations required of these data sources in order to be used for analytics; and the unique 
number of metrics, reports, user interfaces, and predictive models that need to be built out, as well as 
their complexity.  The specific use cases outlined above were used to generate estimates for the first 
two years of this request, with the third and fourth year assuming an equal volume and velocity of use 
cases as the second year.  O&M costs are estimated from existing EDAP O&M costs for prior analytics 
work. 
 
 
5. Conclusion 
 
Con Edison, New York State, and New York City are committed to the most aggressive clean energy 
and climate agenda in the country. As Con Edison works to achieve the ambitious goals set forth by 
various stakeholders, efficient and effective planning becomes indispensable. This is an investment to 
leverage data analytics to support ongoing forecasting and planning efforts as the Company embraces 
a clean energy future.

Work Description: 
The Customer Recommendation and Analysis Tools program is part of the Company’s Strategic 
Customer Experience (“Strategic CX”) Portfolio of projects which seeks to deliver a dynamic customer 
experience that will both meet evolving customer and stakeholder expectations and enable the 
Company to lead the transition to a clean energy future. Additional information about the Company’s 
Strategic CX Portfolio of projects is outlined in the Customer Operations Panel Testimony. 
 
To meet State and local clean energy goals, the Company must expand and enhance its existing clean 
energy webpages and tools to provide customers with a more personalized and interactive experience 
to help customers better engage in the clean energy transition. The Company also needs tools to 
support the contractors and professional networks that directly participate in the Company’s clean 
energy programs and play a key role in facilitating customer adoption of clean energy technologies.  
The Customer Recommendation & Analysis Tools Program (“Program”) will deliver an improved 
online experience by offering a suite of tools, refined by customer sector, to facilitate decision-making 
and adoption of clean energy programs.   
 
CES will use a customer-centric design approach. Through surveys, interviews, and journey mapping, 
customers and contractors will play a key role in the Company’s development of these tools. This 
program will be an ongoing project that will continue to refine the recommendation and analysis tools 
based on customer and stakeholder feedback, clean energy program changes, regulatory changes, and 
technological advances. 
 
The scope of tools provided through the Customer Recommendation and Analysis Tools Program will 
vary to reflect the differing needs and experiences of customers.  Consistent with a “customer first” 
philosophy, each planning phase or “program increment” starts with an examination of feedback from 
customers regarding what they want.   The key focus areas include: 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 15 of 43


--- Page 560 ---
2 
 
 
• 
The Clean Energy Experience:  The Company will provide customers with 
individualized energy savings and clean energy solution recommendations, cost 
estimates, a list of eligible incentives, rate options, and comparisons for mass market 
customers.  Customers will follow a customized digital journey that will allow them to 
input existing home/facility characteristics and technologies through a decision tree 
pathway. They will then receive recommendations of technologies as well as clean 
energy and electrification programs suitable for their home/facility, with an 
understanding of potential bill impacts, the return on investment of these decisions, 
and expected non-energy benefits. As the Company expands the portfolio of rates 
available to mass market customers, additional tools will be needed to help customers 
understand and compare the available rate options. The Company will explore 
expanding the customer-facing tools to include a targeted list of eligible contractors 
who implement the clean energy solution.   
 
Work completed in the rate period would support future development of such as 
providing customers with a summary view of all the Company’s clean energy 
programs that the customer was or is participating in, transparency into the 
customer’s clean energy project status and timeline for payment of program 
incentives, and status updates on any electrification-related upgrades required for Con 
Edison service. 
 
• 
Electrification Experience Hub:  The Company will make significant new investments 
in heating and transport electrification, building envelope upgrades, while also 
addressing electrical constraints to support the State’s clean energy vision.  To enable 
customer adoption, CES will develop digital tools that guide customers through the 
electrification process, while also educating customers on the various technologies and 
potential benefits. The customer’s electrification experience will include service and 
system adequacy estimators for electrification.  To help mitigate potential upgrades, 
the Company will engage with customers on potential options to expedite and/or 
reduce upgrades (e.g., building envelope upgrades that reduce heat pump system 
capacity needs).   
 
• 
Clean Energy Contractor Hub:  Contractors and professionals working with 
customers are critical to meeting State and local clean energy goals.  To support the 
Company’s contractor network, CES plans to develop digital tools that provide 
information about the Company’s clean energy programs, associated rules, project 
application requirements, and incentive amounts.  Through this hub, eligible 
contractors will access Company-approved customer-facing marketing materials, sales 
enablement tools, and updates on their project status and program incentives.   
 
CES will also explore expanding the Contractor Hub to connect contractors with the 
trade professionals and networks necessary to complete clean energy projects, such as 
licensed plumbers and electricians and weatherization contractors.   
 
• 
Clean Energy Customer Service Tools: To advise customers and recommend tailored 
clean energy solutions, Con Edison employees will need additional tools. This includes 
exploring additional Customer Service Representative (“CSR”) tools, business 
development management tools, and tools for the external vendors who manage the 
Company’s clean energy programs.  For example, CSRs and business development 
Exhibit___(IT-5)

3 
 
managers will need tools to access the customer inputs and analyses to respond to any 
customer inquiries regarding customer-specific recommendations.   
 
To implement the Customer Recommendation & Analysis Tools Program, CES must design a roadmap 
detailing the plan for development and roll out.  While the Program has ambitious goals, these 
recommendation and analysis tools will need to be developed in phases for each of the customer and 
contractor segments, as well as through an iterative process to incorporate feedback and adjust to 
changing technologies. To support this endeavor, CES will conduct and complete a Phase 0 analysis in 
2022 with the following detailed assessments: 
• 
Input from key stakeholders including Department of Public Service Staff, customer

•

The Customer Recommendation & Analysis Tools program specifically contributes to these value areas 
because it:

Supports statewide clean energy goals: To achieve the State’s ambitious clean energy goals, the 
Company must not only provide customers with a simple and seamless experience that offers 
customized assessment tools with recommendations, but also improve contractor engagement 
by facilitating their participation in the Company’s programs with easily accessible program 
information and sales enablement tools.  While the current clean energy information and tools 
have expanded gradually over the years, there is need for greater integration and expansion of 
the capabilities.

energy options.

solution recommendations, and rate options/comparisons for mass market customers.  As the

will be needed to help customers understand and compare the available rate options in 
conjunction with their clean energy technology choices. 
 
The Customer Recommendation and Analysis Tools program will help customers overcome the 
complexity of decision-making around clean energy investments and encourage contractor 
participation in the Company’s clean energy programs.  Barriers to customer adoption of clean energy 
solutions will be reduced by providing timing estimates for service and system upgrade needs, along 
with identifying eligible contractors and upgrade mitigation solutions (e.g., energy efficiency building 
envelope).  The Clean Energy Contractor Hub will improve the way the Company offers contractors 
the program information and tools necessary to more effectively market and engage customers.  
Finally, to advise customers and recommend tailored clean energy solutions, Con Edison employees 
will need additional tools. This includes exploring additional Customer Service Representative 
(“CSR”) tools, business development management tools, and tools for the external vendors who 
manage the Company’s clean energy programs.  For example, CSRs and business development 
managers will need tools to access the customer inputs and analyses to respond to any customer 
inquiries regarding customer-specific recommendations.    
 
Industry and societal trends, including technology advances and clean energy policy commitments, 
have and will continue to transform how customers use energy and interact with the Company.  
Supporting customers during the transition to a clean energy economy is at the core of the Company’s 
business and this requires a dynamic customer and contractor experience that will meet evolving and 
enhanced regulatory expectations.  The Customer Recommendation and Analysis Tools program is a 
critical step in leading this transition.

2. Supplemental Information 
 
Alternatives 
Alternative 1 description and reason for rejection 
 
Developing small, one-off, home-grown tools to address the identified customer and company needs. 
This approach is inefficient, as it will result in a lack of cohesiveness and cross-functional coordination 
in the use of Company tools for both customers and contractors.  This approach will impede progress 
toward a clean energy future. Though some individual tools might have a lower cost, collectively they 
would be more costly and less efficient at meeting identified customer / contractor needs. 
 
Alternative 2 description and reason for rejection 
 
Not proceeding with the project. This approach is rejected due to the many identified customer and 
Company needs that must be addressed. 
 
Alternative 3 description and reason for rejection 
 
 
Risk of No Action 
Risk 1 
 
Customer risk. The current lack of these sophisticated, digital tools may lead to customer 
dissatisfaction and frustration. This problem would only be exacerbated as customer expectations 
continue to rise based on digital tool offerings across other industries and as programs and 
technologies become more sophisticated. Customer dissatisfaction, and potential for regulatory 
complaints, will arise if customer needs and expectations are not met.   
 
Risk 2 
 
Clean energy goal achievement.  Many of the solutions needed for a successful clean energy transition 
are unfamiliar to contractors and / or customers.  Without the support of these tools driving customer 
and contractor awareness and consideration, adoption of these solutions may suffer.   
Non-Financial Benefits 
Enhances the customer clean energy experience while enabling achievement of the state’s clean energy 
goals. This solution also enables cross-departmental coordination by developing a set of tools that can 
be used for multiple purposes and programs by those both directly and indirectly supporting the 
Company’s clean energy efforts

for on-going programs the five-year requested amount, including all capital, O&M, retirement.

cost relative to today)

term fixes/maintenance if capital isn’t deployed)

Work Description:  
Con Ed’s service territory currently has 480 MW (40k units with 365 MW of solar) of distributed generation & storage 
The adoption of DER is critical in meeting New York’s carbon reduction goals while providing direct benefits to the 
public including greater customer choices for energy supply, reductions in losses, , decreased reliance on local gas 
generation, reductions in congestion, and local economic development.  The data generated by these assets could enable  
consumers to participate more proactively in the energy market.   However, scaling DER adoption to support The Climate 
Act’s goals is challenging: 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 22 of 43


--- Page 567 ---
• 
Technology:  Several of Con Ed’s systems have finite capacity & capability for the devices they support (e.g., 
SCADA system used for monitoring and control and deeper penetration of DER will increase the data (e.g., live 
telemetry reads from more devices) that will be needed to manage the grid reliably.   
• 
Processes:  Many processes for managing, connecting, and registering DER today are manual (e.g., review of 
interconnection screens, data transfer/entry between systems).  Manual processes will not be able to timely meet 
future customer demands as DER penetration grows and will be viewed as barriers preventing achievement of 
the Climate Act’s requirements.   
• 
Grid Planning & Operation: Today, several circuits are at hosting capacity limits (DER penetration has been 
high) where adding new DER would be cost prohibitive (e.g., in Staten Island and Westchester). Better tools for 
planning and operating DER can unlock some of this capacity, allowing more DER to interconnect in these areas. 
An increase in DER penetration may also make the power supply profile increasingly variable, thus adding 
complexity to safety, grid stability, asset condition, reliability, and resilience. 
The DER Integration and Management program will address these challenges and improve hosting capacity, 
resiliency, market access, long term grid capital cost, and DER customer experience for both individual users and 3rd party 
aggregators (see the Justification section).  To achieve this, Con Ed must build new capabilities.  In the near-term, Con Ed 
will accelerate the deployment of new capabilities where there is a high confidence of immediate value while capabilities 
requiring  further review and analysis will be pursued via a smaller scale minimum viable product (MVP) development to 
assess the use case  
We will solve for 11 use cases: 
(1) Improvements in the hosting capacity process, analysis, and maps;  
(2) Increases in the automation of the CESIR study process;  
(3)  Increases in the ability to validate DER data between the registration and interconnection databases;  
(4) Automation of monthly updates to the hosting capacity map;  
(5) Increases in the ability to assess long-term load forecasting/grid hosting constraints on a time-series level;  
(6) Enhances real-time power flow and distribution-level demand response modelling, incorporating DER and weather;  
(7) Enhances communication with DER owners / aggregators and other demand side resources;  
(8) Incentivizing customers to select the “best” locations with ‘search and find’ capabilities;  
(9) Automation of the connection of DER status, controllability, and characteristics to load flow planning; 
(10) Acquiring the ability to implement push DER / inverter settings to align with seasonal operating regime; and  
(11) Acquiring control of grid edge assets in case of localized disruptions & maintenance/external adverse events.   
To meet these challenges, additional investments are required over the next three years.   These investments center on 
three areas related to IT/OT software and infrastructure, grid edge technology, and a smart inverter customer program. 
Information Systems & Operational Software 
The IT / OT software and infrastructure investments center on seven discrete initiatives: 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 23 of 43


--- Page 568 ---
(1) The development of an online grid-edge DER nameplate database; 
(2) The development of a middleware translation platform; 
(3) A custom-built solution for network flow modeling integrating PVL (Poly-voltage load flow)  that considers DER and 
weather; 
(4) Linking historical database of DER behavior to PVL tool;  
(5) Development of a unified control dashboard used for system switching (coordinated with NYISO) and system 
planning (load flow analysis, outage scheduling, work prioritization); and  
(6) Various improvements to Cybersecurity systems. 
Grid Edge Technology Environment: 
This area involves adding capabilities to The Learning Center (“TLC”) for testing & deployment of the four MVP level 
use cases in a simulated environment without impacting operations.  The TLC would feature both sample grid-edge devices 
(e.g., EV chargers, smart inverters) and a simulated control center (including representative Con Ed IT/OT stack).  In the 
short term, it will allow Con Ed to better understand the value of the MVP capabilities Con Ed is building out and provide 
the ability to train employees in a simulated environment.  In the longer term, this asset will be leveraged to develop the 
next horizon of capabilities such as advances in sensors, high-speed/volume communications, edge computing, predictive 
analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI) bringing incremental value to customers. In addition, the findings of the Grid Edge 
Tech Environment will allow Con Ed to collaborate with community and vendor stakeholders, to ensure an equitable 
renewable transition. 
Smart inverter customer program: 
Con Ed is requesting regulatory asset funding to cover inverter upgrade costs for customers.. This will enable customer 
participation in MVP development that will bring wide reaching benefits The Smart inverter program should help unlock 
hosting capacity, improve the customer experience, and lower long-term T&D costs. 
The expected cost of these investments is as follows (more detail to follow in the cost section of this document):

Justification Summary: 
The justification for Con Ed’s investment in comprehensive distributed energy resource integration and management is 
based on enablement of five key short- and long-term benefits: (1) scaling the hosting capacity of the distribution grid, (2) 
preparing the system for new markets, (3) improving the DER ownership experience, (4) lowering the long-term cost of the 
energy transition, and (5) maintaining system reliability & resiliency.  In this rate case, Con Ed will make investments 
focusing  on enabling benefits and solving challenges in the next 3 -5 years.  This timeframe primarily addresses the first 
three areas of benefit while the benefits related to the latter two items will be unlocked in the future through deployment of 
abilities being developed at the MVP level in this rate case: 
1. Scale system hosting capacity to meet New York city and state climate targets 
 
.. Absent investments supporting the capabilities described above, there will be significant challenges over the next 3 – 5 
years in areas where hosting capacity is already exceeded (e.g., parts of Staten Island and Westchester) as well as other areas 
that will face similar situations as DER adoption grows.   
 
Several of the capabilities noted in the Work Description will mitigate the recent increases in interconnection costs. The  
need for feeder extensions and service upgrades can be reduced with more accurate hosting capacity abilities and increasing 
automation of the hosting capacity analysis process.  This would provide customers more accurate circuit visibility for project 
planning through improve the hosting capacity analyses that take place more frequently, with fewer assumptions, and at a 
more granular circuit level. The ability to assess load forecasting/grid hosting constraints at a time-series level would also 
limit the need for network protector improvements.    
 
In the longer term, the ability to monitor and remotely control smart inverter settings will increase circuit hosting 
capacity by decreasing the need for SCADA hardware and voltage regulation at DER sites. Additionally, the ability to 
automatically adjust smart inverter settings based on circuit conditions (e.g., voltage control, fault response settings) may 
further Con Ed’s ability to unlock hosting capacity without materially impacting DER revenues.  
 
 
Finally, as DER proliferates, a monitoring system is needed to provide cheaper scaling while maintaining the highest 
levels of cybersecurity.   The SCADA Distributed Network Protocol (DNP3) system is primarily used for communication 
between a master station and remote terminal units/intelligent electronic devices, allocates points to monitor large grid-edge 
assets’ live statuses and characteristics and as such is not suited for the challenges of the future.. This new system  will enable 
use of a scalable ‘middleman’ distributed intelligent intermediary system preventing direct communication between 
customer DER equipment and Con Ed central systems, to avoid potential cybersecurity challenges. 
 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 25 of 43


--- Page 570 ---
2. System preparation for new market architectures 
 
A value driver of DER ownership is the ability of the DER owner to sell energy and other grid services.  FERC 2222 
permits DER owners to participate in the wholesale market. While this benefits DER owners, it increases the complexity of 
communication between utilities, DER customers / aggregators, and the NYISO.  To ensure safe and reliable grid operations, 
the NYISO envisions distribution system operators having the ability to notify aggregators when an individual asset must be 
derated / forced out of service based on current grid conditions (e.g., load profile). While today, most DER can discharge 
without posing issues, increasing amounts of DER responding concurrently to a NYISO dispatch signal, may create capacity 
and voltage issues, resulting in voltage levels outside ANSI limitations. Building out the ability to model real time power 
flow and distribution-level demand response with DER will enable more agile decisions about when output must be 
restricted while maximizing DER utilization.   
 
In the longer term, there is potential to host the distribution-level market platform with auctions for localized 
“distribution” services from aggregated DER. This forward-looking capability would create additional value streams for DER 
participants while building grid resiliency and flexibility through holding and producing dispatchable energy.  
 
3. Improve the DER ownership experience 
 
To drive deep DER adoption in its service territory, Con Ed is focused on providing the best possible customer 
experience for planning, interconnecting, registering, and operating a DER. Historically, utilities in other states with 
advanced DER adoption rates (e.g., Hawaii, California) have faced challenges scaling their interconnection processes to meet 
demand, such that interconnection has become a bottleneck to rapid DER adoption1. Con Ed seeks to proactively address 
existing and growing challenges in the customer journey through by making investments that mitigate current challenges. To 
achieve these goals, Con Ed must invest in key capabilities related to hosting capacity analysis/mapping, process 
automation, and data validation/streamlining.  .  
 
During DER developers’ initial project planning process, there are gaps in visibility into circuit hosting capacity 
including: (1) the lack of a hosting capacity analysis for 1 or 2-phase circuits which comprise the majority of DER 
applications; (2) the hosting capacity analysis assumption of an even load distribution across non-meshed loops;  (3) the use 
of a generic shoulder month minimum load without circuit-specific DER information; and (4) the manual monthly update of 
customer-facing hosting capacity maps. Data import automation and increasing granularity of hosting capacity analyses 
through technology that enhances data availability and modeling capabilities can address these matters.  
 
While Con Ed is compliant with current statewide interconnection requirements, there are opportunities to shorten the 
process (currently up to 80 days are allowed), increase transparency to applicants, and better align customer expectations 
with final interconnection costs.  Interconnection application times and costing accuracy can be improved by working to 
automate and increase capacity of the CESIR studies, automate manual data entry in the ‘applicant options’ phase, and the 
aforementioned improvements to hosting capacity maps.  
 
 
1 Source: Hawaii PUC—"Opening a Proceeding to Review Hawaiian Electric’s Interconnection Process and Transition Plans for Retirement 
of Fossil Fuel Power Plants” (2021) 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 26 of 43


--- Page 571 ---
Con Ed can also improve the DER ownership experience by investing in tools to validate customer asset information 
between the interconnection and market registration steps to flag inconsistencies early, reduce the probability of customers 
needing to troubleshoot later issues with billing or curtailment, and ensure that DER registrations actually can provide the 
registered generation / storage capacity.   
 
Finally, in the longer-term Con Ed’s requested funding for MVP development will incentivize DER build out in areas 
where they are valuable to the grid. In addition the development of the MVP smart inverter program settings for testing, 
eventually rolling out at scale longer-term to allow for voltage management (e.g., Volt-Var control, fixed power factor), bulk 
system support (e.g., voltage ride-through, frequency ride through), and communication & interactivity (e.g., configuration, 
R/T feedback).  
 
4. Lower long-term cost of the energy transition 
 
In the long term, the transition to renewable energy sources will increase costs due to the required grid upgrades. 
Customer energy costs can potentially be lowered by empowering customers to make more informed decisions related to 
their power consumption and timing. Although these benefits are further in the future, as part of the DER Integration and 
Management program, Con Ed will begin building out MVP functionality in the Grid-Edge Technology Environment (e.g., 
smart inverter setting control) to lay the groundwork for delivering them.  
Con Ed must maintain system reliability and resiliency as the DER buildout continues.  Con Ed’s systems must ensure 
adequate energy supply and load flow, considering both variability in DER supply and potentially price-elastic DER 
demand. To minimize customer disruptions to power flow on the grid caused by DER, distribution planning processes must  
incorporate DER capacity and monitor DER asset statuses in relation to projected load flow.

This program supports dynamic distribution system management and optimization to enable the smart grid of the future and 
the company’s role as a DSP.

2. Supplemental Information 
 
Alternatives: 
     An alternative is continued use of point-to-point system connections between discrete systems. Maintaining and 
enhancing this alternative is costly as every new functionality can require multiple system integrations and will not enable 
the future capabilities required operationally for customers.  A point-to-point connection architecture also imposes a ceiling 
constraint for automation and real-time capabilities based on the latency of collecting data in various systems, verifying it, 
and presenting it to operators.  This limitation will be exacerbated as DER penetration grows.   
Risk of No Action: 
Without near-term investment by Con Ed in a DER integration & management program, DER adoption will experience delays 
in service territories, potentially limiting progress toward CLCPA goals.   
• 
Reduced hosting capacity: There are already some hosting capacity restrictions in the highest growth areas (e.g., 
Staten Island) which are expected to expand as DER adoption increases.  Without the sophisticated modeling 
capabilities for which funding is requested in this rate case, limitations may exist in terms of the solutions provided to 
customers as an alternative to costly infrastructure buildout. 
• 
Longer interconnection times & limited transparency AS  DER going through the interconnection process increase, 
bottlenecks in the interconnection process will become more acute and costly without the proposed investments.   
• 
Limited ability to enable new market participation: Alongside capabilities developed by the NYISO and REV/DPS 
staff, Con Ed has been building out MVP capabilities to enable market participation as laid out by FERC 2222 but will 
need to build out enterprise level capabilities to support broad market participation as envisioned by the NYISO.  
Non-financial Benefits: 
 
      In the near term, the Work Description capabilities will improve customer experience, increase hosting capacity, and 
enabling participation in the wholesale markets;  all non-financial benefits

4. Basis for estimate 
 
The landscape of DERMS technology offerings is rapidly evolving and changing, with regard to how DERMS modules and 
systems fit into legacy platforms and future ADMS systems. Furthermore, Con Ed’s systems differ from those of other utilities 
(e.g., custom-built PVL tool used for mesh network modeling). Given these uncertainties, several sources were drawn from to 
generate the investment cost estimate:  
• 
Vendor quotes for specific DERMS components (e.g., from Oracle) 
• 
e.g., Gartner, Forrester) 
• 
Previous similar efforts undertaken by Con Ed (e.g., DERMS MVP deployment) 
The potential for future cloud-based systems was also included in estimates, as well as required data governance initiatives. 
In 2022, Con Ed will embark on a process of receiving detailed competitive bids to further refine these numbers. 
5. Conclusion 
Additional dollars will be justified for the DER integration & management program. These investments will allow Con Ed to 
improve its ability to anticipate changes, particularly regarding the timing, nature and magnitude of customer technology 
adoption and grid impacts.   These investments are also expected to address several near-term challenges while bringing 
additional benefits to customers.  Specifically: 
1. The project will bring significant near- and long-term benefits to New Yorkers: As detailed in the Justification, this 
program will unlock five key benefits: (1) scaling the hosting capacity of the distribution grid, (2) preparing the 
system for new markets, (3) improving the DER ownership experience, (4) lowering the long-term cost of the energy 
transition, and (5) maintaining system reliability & resiliency.  In the short term, increased hosting capacity, access to 
new markets, and improved customer experience will be felt the most acutely, however, in the longer-term Con Ed 
expects to see benefits across all five of these categories. 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 29 of 43


--- Page 574 ---
2. The risk of no action is high: Without these investments, New York City and Westchester county’s abilities to drive 
increased DER adoption toward the goals laid out in the Climate Act and elsewhere will be limited.  
3. The phased approach being taken by Con Ed prioritizes addressing near term needs while laying a long-term 
foundation:   Making foundational investments today allows acceleration of the deployment of critical grid future 
technologies and integrate new tools and grid planning processes to lower deployment time, harmonize current grid 
operations with future needs and make more adaptive decisions.

Technical Evaluation/ Analysis 
 
 Con Ed expects to continue tracking existing KPIs (e.g., DER capacity on the system, # of DER assets on the system) to 
measure the effects of DER buildout on existing systems, as well as measure the ability of new investments to address various 
levels of DER buildout. To explore ways of improving the DER participant experience, Con Ed will continue to track the 
average customer time spent in the interconnection process , the accuracy of the interconnection cost estimate, and the 
average final customer interconnection cost-per-kW of project capacity. Finally, as FERC 2222 is rolled out, Con Ed will 
internally track the percent of DER enrolled and participating in the wholesale market. 
As part of this program, Con Ed will develop four MVP level use cases to inform the progression of these systems, 
capabilities, and future rate requests. To support this effort, Con Ed will track and collect data to allow intelligent assessment 
of the value of wider deployment of these capabilities. The outcome measurement for each of those use cases is as follows: 
• 
For the ability to incentivize customers to select value-add project geography and capacity, improvements to the customer 
project planning process will be tracked, as well as any changes to project cancellation rates 
• 
For developing capabilities to automate the connection of DER live-status and characteristics to the load flow planning 
process, the cost to monitor necessary asset data from each DER will be tracked and compared to traditional (e.g., 
SCADA) asset monitoring costs 
• 
For the ability to dynamically adjust smart inverter settings, benefits pertaining to either customer energy costs or 
improvements to customer experience will be tracked and compared against a control use case 
• 
For the ability to control assets at the grid edge in order to remedy local disruptions, ability to decrease outage time based 
on locally deployed dispatchable capacity will be tracked

Work Description: 
Con Edison (“the Company”) is  investing in the design and operation of the Distributed System Platform (“DSP”). 
Our DSP enables functionality in key areas of Electric System (“Grid”) functions, like Integrated Planning, 
Distributed Energy Resources (“DER”) Integration and Grid Operations as well as Grid Services such as Market 
Services and Relationship Management for customers. The DSP is the foundation for the people, process, 
technology, and infrastructure evolution to meet the goals set forth in the New York State Climate Leadership and 
Consumer Protection Act (“CLCPA”). In addition, the DSP is a foundational driver for longer term electrification 
and de-carbonization goals that will require a modern, optimized grid that not only enables bi-directional energy 
flow and manages the intermittency of load and supply but unlocks renewable technologies. Additionally, a core 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 34 of 43


--- Page 579 ---
tenet of the DSP evolution will continue to increase resiliency in step with the Company’s recent Climate Change 
Vulnerability Study while maintaining the safety and reliability standards expected by our customers.  
The 2016, 2018 and 2020 DSIPs captured DSP functionality in three key areas: DER Integration, Information Sharing 
and Market Services. Across all these grid functions and services, Con Edison remains focused on the desired 
outcomes of the present and future DSP: Addressing interconnection issues, increasing hosting capacity and 
reducing curtailments, optimizing Grid edge operations and creating value for both DER and customers at the grid 
edge.   
Con Edison currently operates and maintains an Interconnection Online Application Portal (“IOAP”), Hosting 
Capacity Maps, and Green Button Connect (“GBC”) for data sharing.  The Company also manages a Demand 
Response Management System (“DRMS”) to manage aggregators, aggregations, and Demand Response (“DR”) 
programs that provide system relief during reliability events. These investments provide the foundation for the 
DSP to incorporate DERs into the existing electric grid and establish long term planning processes for grid 
modernization and DER deployment.  However, incremental investment in these areas is needed to fully integrate 
DER value in the existing grid while creating the operational flexibility and resilience necessary to realize the 
CLCPA vision. Additional investments will drive outcomes in the following categories: integrated planning, DER 
integration, grid modernization, market services, and managing customer relationships. 
1) DER Integration  
 
Interconnection Online Application Portal  
One core component required for timely interconnection is the IOAP. Con Edison maintains an IOAP to facilitate 
timely DER interconnection processes (www.coned.com/dg), which now uses the PowerClerk tool as well as 
enhancements to its case management tool, the Customer Project Management System (“CPMS”).  The IOAP design 
includes elements of the Electric Power Research Institute (“EPRI”) IOAP evaluation and phased approach, of 
which, Con Edison completed Phase 1 in October 2017. These changes offered more granularity and transparency 
to the customer during the Standardized Interconnection Requirements (“SIR”) process and automated many of 
the screens, data exchanges and processing steps that increased transparency in application processing. Additional 
investments in the IOAP will allow the company to continue building automations to support and maintain 
compliance with the evolving SIR process. Enhancements are focused on; administrative updates associated with 
the SIR, shortening timelines associated with document review, screening processes, engineering studies and 
program support. The Company will also continue to link and refine data sets across systems. These activities are 
a core input to the Hosting Capacity and grid analysis that both helps the utility understand the current system 
dynamics as well as better forecast and plan grid enhancements that may be needed in areas of increasing 
penetration. An example of this can be seen below in the way that Network Protector Relay programs are structured 
and optimized.  
 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 35 of 43


--- Page 580 ---
2) Grid Modernization  
 
Modernize Network Protector (“NWP”) Relays 
Most NWPs are equipped with a non-communicating microprocessor relay (“MPR”). Non-communicating MPRs 
are designed to identify when a reverse power flow condition exists, such as when DG provides power to the grid. 
Such instances cause the associated NWP to automatically trip. When an NWP does not trip the feeder remains 
alive-on-backfeed (“ABF”).  Depending on system conditions, a feeder can remain ABF anywhere from a few cycles 
to hours. Troubleshooting ABF conditions delays feeder processing. In addition, ABF conditions that follow a single 
line-to-ground fault can cause the voltage on the unfaulted phases to increase by as much as 73 percent. The 
Company’s internal analysis has shown that there is a correlation between this rise in voltage and faults on the 
unfaulted phases, known as second faults.  As DER penetration increases, there will be more persistent challenges, 
which create unnecessary and avoidable costs to the system and therefore to customers.  
The Company will continue to modernize protective relays. This grid modernization effort, begun in 2017, provides 
Network Protectors (“NWP”) the intelligence to distinguish DG back feed from fault current. This capability 
increases the Company ability to accommodate cleaner solar and helps eliminate one of the more common 
interconnection costs in areas where this functionality is present. In addition to the relaying upgrades, the Company 
has prioritized certain locations for SCADA enabled communications to allow remote operation and control to 
eliminate conditions referred to as alive on backfeed (“ABF”) where a NWP can fail to open for several hours, 
thereby effecting the efficiency of the local network. To date, the Company has replaced 3,829 relays with 1,336 of 
these equipped with SCADA capability out of approximately 27,000 NWP in the secondary grid. The Company 
plans to continue this program in an effort to address each location that is or becomes Distributed Generation 
constrained as well as all locations with persistent ABF issues.   
Smart Grid Optimization  
Con Edison is continuing the Conservation Voltage Optimization (“CVO”) efforts as part of the Smart Grid 
Optimization efforts in 2022.    The primary purpose of CVO is to reduce energy costs and environmental impacts 
while continuing to maintain acceptable voltage at all points along the distribution feeder under all loading 
conditions.  
Based on the Company’s efforts implementing CVO technologies to date, the Company is on track to achieve its 
CVO energy savings goals. Operating the system at optimal voltages reduces total energy consumption and 
associated power generation emissions, resulting in significant energy savings for our customers and a reduced 
carbon footprint.  
In 2023-2025, the objective of this request is to accelerate and exceed the CVO schedule to increase the energy 
savings to 1.75 percent by the end of 2025 and, as a result, realize an additional $75.8 million Net Present Value 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 36 of 43


--- Page 581 ---
(“NPV”) in net energy savings through 2042 that will reduce the supply side costs of the customer bill while 
further reducing GHG emissions. 
3) Investments in this area will allow the requisite equipment and system upgrades needed to perform these 
optimized voltage operations. Market Services  
 
Demand Management Tracking System (“DMTS”): DMTS provides the Company with the necessary technology 
infrastructure to track and manage the performance of the Company’s Energy Efficiency and Demand management 
(“EEDM”) portfolio goals, and streamline the payment of incentives to customers participating in the Department’s 
energy efficiency and building electrification programs. Since 2020, the EEDM Department has completed 
implementation of a number of new programs into DMTS (e.g., Clean Heat, MF Low and Moderate Income), 
integrated DRMS into its approval and payment process (see below), provide energy savings calculations, and 
created tools for participating contractors to estimate the financial support they can receive for energy efficiency 
upgrades prior to submitting project applications.  Additional investments will be required in the DMTS to support 
program expansion functionality and market development as the Company launches new programs, offers new 
energy efficiency or building electrification measures, and provides new kinds of program incentive structures to 
promote greater market engagement and customer participation.   
Investments will expand customer participation and improve opportunities for energy savings and demand 
reduction across existing and future programs.  This includes enhancing incentive estimation tools and decreasing 
the time from application submission to project payment. 
 DRMS: DRMS supports the management of enrollment, event initiation, performance monitoring, and settlement 
of the Company’s DR programs. This system enables Con Edison to efficiently interact with customers enrolled in 
DR programs and manage peak demand.  DR resources, an integral subset of DER portfolios, are used to lower 
network peaks on peak summer days as well as to alleviate operational contingencies.  The DR programs are 
designed to help defer other traditional capital investments.  
The DRMS is a key operating tool used to support a portfolio of DR programs, which have substantially grown 
over 300% in customer enrollment from 2020 to 2021 within the CSRP, DLRP, Term-DLM, Auto-DLM, and Non-
Wires programs the DRMS supports. As these programs grow in number and complexity, they will require 
enhancements as well as the flexibility to adapt to changes in tariff rules.   Enhancements will include expanded 
enrollment capabilities as more residential and small commercial customers participate in aggregator enrollments.  
ConnectDER: In response to New York State Energy Research and Development (“NYSERDA”) Future Grid 
Challenge, Con Ed and ConnectDER collaborated on a project to develop solutions to integrate clean and renewable 
energy into the electric grid.  Con Edison and ConnectDER were selected via a competitive solicitation process and 
awarded $2.3M to support the execution costs of the project. In order to maximize efficiency and better serve 
customers, Con Ed regularly evaluates new forecasting and monitoring technologies. DER’s penetration is growing 
every day and impacts the net load the Company serves; as a result, it is becoming more important to forecast DER 
at granular levels that account for output, correlation with net load, and geographical effects.  The objective of the 
Exhibit___(IT-5)
Page 37 of 43


--- Page 582 ---
project is to increase the existing electric grid’s capabilities to serve load and integrate distributed renewables while 
reducing distribution costs to consumer and system upgrades to achieve New York’s aggressive decarbonization 
goals and statewide scale-up of renewable energy resources. This project will help enhance grid reliability and 
integrate renewables by installing 2,400 ConnectDER devices at identified customer locations within Con Ed’s 
territory. Additionally, a core tenet of market services and the DSP is information sharing. A more granular 
understanding of the system dynamics at the grid edge will  
Justification Summary: 
 
Con Edison has created a foundational DSP that continues to integrate DER, compiles and shares increasingly 
complex information and identifies areas within the electric grid where modern solutions can create the requisite 
system flexibility to increase hosting capacity and operate a safe and reliable electric system while accommodating 
increased penetration of DER. Further investment in this platform will continue to leverage this foundation and 
increase the capabilities in the areas of system planning, DER integration and system operation to create more 
optimization and opportunity at the grid edge. These advancements continue to drive DER adoption as a core tenet 
of utility practice and are necessary to accelerate the transition to a more flexible distribution grid that will achieve 
state energy goals.   
Relationship to Broader Company Plans and Initiatives (e.g. Long-Range Plans, CLCPA Initiatives, Risk Mitigation) 
The DSP is a critical element to Con Edison delivering on our Clean Energy Commitment that includes “100% 
Clean Electricity by 2040.”  Enabling these grid edge and customer facing tools will continue to create the system 
flexibility needed to transition towards a clean energy future and achieve state goals.

4. Definitions  
 
Total Funding Request: All funding requested for program or project over program/project lifecycle, including all 
capital, O&M, retirement, and contingency expenses. 
 
Total Contingency: Total contingency expense according to the Corporate Contingency Guidelines 
 
Cost Savings: Reductions in costs that are currently being incurred (e.g., reduced annual maintenance cost relative to 
today) 
 
Cost Avoidance: Reductions in anticipated future costs that don’t occur today (e.g., anticipated short-term fixes if capital 
isn’t replaced)

Work Description: 
  
This project implements the recommendations of the Gas Transaction System Replacement Phase 0 project. The 
recommended solution must meet the requirements of purchasing, scheduling, accounting for and reporting of physical 
gas transactions. 
Justification Summary: 
 
The IGS system is the main tool to manage the Company's gas portfolio.  The system must be maintained and flexible to 
meet the changing market and economic conditions as well as meeting new marketer programs being proposed. 
• 
Energy Management's Gas Supply Department processes approximately $1 billion in wholesale gas 
transactions, and requires a supportable software platform to track and schedule energy transactions, as well as 
perform proper risk oversight functions.  
• 
The Gas Supply business changes frequently and requires a flexible platform to accommodate new business 
opportunities. 
• 
The proposed solution should provide additional opportunities for automating accounting functions such as 
Accounts Payable (AP), Accounts Receivable (AR), and General Ledger (GL). 
• 
Energy Management and Energy Risk Management are frequent areas of audits, and require strict compliance 
with Sarbanes Oxley (SOX) controls, and audit capabilities.

• 
The gas industry is rapidly changing and the company requires updated software to ensure flexibility to 
participate in new markets and products. The proposed solutions should enable the Company to take 
advantage of industry best practices based on input from other utilities and market participants.
